Is there a general relationship between the seagrass Zostera noltii biomass and the field spectroradiometer readings?

Lee, Chengfa Benjamin

18 December 2025 (last updated on 14 janvier 2026)

This study aims to establish a relationship between the amount of biomass and reflectance of the Zostera noltii seagrass.

1 Method

This data exploration uses the hyperspectral and biomass data collected during these field campaigns in Aveiro (July 2025), Bourgneuf Bay (2018, 2019, and September 2025), and Cadiz Bay (June 2025).

1.1 Hyperspectral data

For each sample, the hyperspectral signature was smoothed with a rolling average (size = 11) using the rollapply() function from the zoo package (Zeileis and Grothendieck 2005). While this means that the first and last five wavelengths would be smoothed with a partial moving window of less than 11 values, given the spectroradiometer’s full wavelength range of 325nm to 1075nm and the final working range of 400nm to 900nm, these affected wavelengths will be filtered out and thus irrelevant here.

Post-smoothing, only the wavelengths from 400nm to 900nm are retained and a min-max standardisation was performed.

1.2 Biomass data

Full methods can be found here.

1.3 Carbon content data

The dried leaf (aboveground biomass, AGB) and root (belowground biomass, BGB) biomass were pulverised prior to the measurement of total carbon (TC) and inorganic carbon (IC) content in fly ash using a SSM-5000A Shimadzu Solid Sample Combusion Unit. To measure the TC content in a sample, about 70 g of powdered biomass is combusted at 900°C for 8 minutes. For the IC content measurement, about 300 g of powdered biomass is mixed with 0.9 ml of phosphorous acid (HPO3) and combusted at 300°C until no carbon dioxide is detected. The measurements are scaled to the total weight of the samples using Equation (1). The difference between the TC and IC is the total organic carbon content (TOC).

\[\begin{equation} Carbon\,concentration\,(g\,per\,C/kg) = \frac{Measured\,Carbon\,(mg) \times Dry\,Weight\,(\%) \times 1000}{Wet\,weight\,of\,essay\,(mg)} \tag{1} \end{equation}\]

1.4 General relationship between reflectance and biomass

As the relationship established using the hyperspectral data will be applied onto the Sentinel-2 (S2) image, the hyperspectral data needs to be translated to be equivalent to S2. This was explored and optimised in two ways:

  • Using the centre (Zoffoli et al. 2020) vs the peak wavelength of S2A bands, based on the S2 Spectral Response Function Document: COPE-GSEG-EOPG-TN-15-0007
  • Testing three different vegetative indices, based on the comparison by Bargain et al. (2013)
    • Normalised Difference Vegetative Index (NDVI)
    • Atmospherically-Resistant Vegetative Index (ARVI)
    • Modified Normalised Difference Index equivalent to the B5 and B6 bands of S2 (mND)

While there were no significant difference in predictive performance between the centre and peak band wavelength, the latter was slightly better. For brevity, the results henceforth are based on the peak wavelength of the S2 bands.

Similarly, the indices performed similarly. NDVI is the only index here that uses only the 10m spatial resolution bands, unlike the ARVI and mND which rely on the 20m spatial resolution coastal band. Therefore, NDVI was selected as the optimal index.

1.5 Accuracy Assessment

The adjusted R2, root mean square error (RMSE), and relative/normalised RMSE were used to assess the performance of the linear models. The adjusted R2 was obtained from the stat_regline_equation() function in the ggpubr package (Kassambara 2025). RMSE was obtained from the lm() function in the stats package (R Core Team 2025). The relative RMSE was obtained by dividing the RMSE with the mean of the independent variable.

For the non-linear model, residual standard error (RSE) was used to inspect the fit of the exponential curve. the RSE was obtained from the nls() function in the stats package (R Core Team 2025).

2 Result

2.1 Biomass

The matchup between the leaf and root biomass seemed linear in relationship up to about 100 g/m2, before a saturation was reached. There is a total of 9 saturated stations, all from Cadiz (Figure 1).

Figure 1: Scatterplot of leaf biomass (AGB) to root biomass (BGB) of Zostera noltii across all sites. While this matchup seems to be linear for much of the dataset, there are 9 stations in Cadiz with very high AGB and BGB that suggests a saturation. Thus, an exponential curve was fitted. For the linear model, the saturated points were removed to estimate the linear relationship up to saturation. Owing to some stations having no seagrass AGB and BGB, 20 data points are overlapping at the plot origin (0,0).

Thus, the saturated points were excluded from the dataset to obtain a linear relationship (Figure 2, Adj. R2 = 0.59, RMSE = 19.5).

Figure 2: A zoomed-in look at the scatterplot of leaf biomass (AGB) to root biomass (BGB) of Zostera noltii across all sites, excluding the very high biomass (saturated) data points in Cadiz. The RMSE for this model is in the table below.

2.2 Hyperspectral data

Generally, the greater the dry weight, the lower the reflectance at the individual sites (Figure 3 and Figure 4). This is most evident with the Cadiz sites, which are split by seagrass percent cover, which is a proxy of biomass here. In particular, the absorption at around 670 nm (S2 red band) is greater with more seagrass AGB.

Figure 3: Raw spectroradiometer reflectance measurements compared against the dry weight (g/m2).

Figure 4: Min-max standardised spectroradiometer reflectance measurements compared against the dry weight (g/m2).

2.4 General relationship between the reflectance and biomass

Similar to the matchup between AGB and BGB, there is a saturation of the NDVI at higher AGB (> 200 g/m2) (Bargain et al. 2013).

Figure 5: Scatterplot of spectroradiometer-derived NDVI to seagrass leaf biomass. An exponential curve was fitted to the dataset. By removing the saturated points (AGB > 200 g/m2), a linear relationship can be obtained up to the estimated point of saturation.

A linear relationship was established between the spectroradiometer-derived NDVI and the seagrass leaf biomass (Figure 6, Adj. R2 = 0.62, RMSE = 21.8) up to 200 g/m2 in AGB.

Figure 6: A zoomed-in look at the scatterplot of spectroradiometer-derived NDVI to seagrass leaf biomass. The RMSE for this model is in the table below.
